events.title: The capital's lamps lit late and few
events.body: With coal-fuel dear, the lamp-men of Cathair dhearg light the street-lamps later in the evening and put them out earlier in the night, and light fewer of them in the lanes behind the fish-quays and under the walls. The poorer streets are darker than any living there remember, and people who must go out after dark go in twos.

events.title: The shires' chests counted
events.body: The copyists of Leabharlann Muileann chaol finish the lists of the shires' record-chests called in over the years before, and Ailig mac Thormoid brings the chronicler the tally: one thousand and six chests. The chest of Seann Tarr, burned in its own yard, is entered as sent. The fourth floor of the new wing stands empty.

events.title: Coal-fuel sold above the fair's ceiling
events.body: All summer the dealers at Fèill Muileann òg sell coal-fuel above the ceiling the court of the fair has fixed. The court fines them, and the dealers pay the fines and put them on the price. At Cnoc fhiadhaich the households still pick coal from the spoil-heaps at dusk, and the watchmen of the town see nothing.

events.title: The black cake at the Caol mhòr market
events.body: A Tuathach pedlar brings a cake of a black fuel made from pit waste to the market at Caol mhòr and shows it burning. Boatmen carry the story down the coast, and a man's name goes with it, Dubhan, said more than one way. Nothing of the fuel is bought or sold.

events.title: The carrier's word on the library road
events.body: Dòmhnall mac Ailein, carrier on the library road, brings to Muileann chaol a drover's report, had from a boatman out of Caol mhòr, of a fuel made in the north from what the pits throw away, which burns like coal and stinks. Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh enters it in her own day-book with the man's name given two ways.

events.title: The keeper's word at an Leabharlann
events.body: Asked by the chronicler what is to be done about the report of a fuel in the north, Raghnall mac Mhuirich, keeper of Leabharlann Muileann chaol, answers that if the thing is real someone will write it down and send the writing, and that an Leabharlann keeps and does not chase.

events.title: The fuel burned at the Muileann chaol market
events.body: On the market day in the yard of an Leabharlann a Tuathach pedlar of needles and lace burns a piece of the black fuel on the flagstone by the pump. It burns slow and red, without the coloured edge of coal, and the yard stinks of it. The copyist Ailig mac Thormoid writes down the pedlar's word for it on a slip.

events.title: The chronicler at the ford
events.body: Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh walks down from an Leabharlann to the ford at Àth dhomhain after the pedlar, and learns from the ferryman's boy that he waded over at noon and went on towards the landing at Ceann dhomhain and the boats south. She does not see the fuel.

events.title: Beathag's letter to the maor of Caol mhòr
events.body: The chronicler writes to the maor of Caol mhòr that a fuel made from pit waste is reported out of the north, and asks for a piece of it by the carrier, with a line saying where it came from and who made it. The letter goes north under the office's seal. No answer comes.

events.title: The autumn rains on the library road
events.body: At the end of an Dàmhair the first rains of the autumn come in from the west after the dry summer. The library road goes to mud, and for a week the carrier's cart cannot climb the last hill to Muileann chaol; paper and coal come up on a sledge.

events.title: The coal of an Leabharlann cut
events.body: The winter's coal for Leabharlann Muileann chaol comes up less than the year before and dearer. Raghnall mac Mhuirich orders no fire in the reading-room before the middle of an t-Samhain and none after dark, and the copyists who would work in the evenings take their copying home.

events.title: The day of binding at Achadh dhomhain passes empty
events.body: At Achadh dhomhain the masters of Comann nan Gualadairean sit an hour on the day of binding with the oath-stone before them, and no family brings a son or daughter to be bound. The clerk writes the day into the book with nothing under it.

events.title: The fourth floor at Muileann chaol still empty
events.body: Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh and the copyist Ailig mac Thormoid walk the new wing of an Leabharlann. The shires' chests fill three floors; the fourth, left for what was not sent, stands swept and bare.

events.title: Seann Tarr entered as sent to the fire
events.body: On the keeper's order the copyists enter the shire chest of Seann Tarr, burned in the yard by its keeper rather than sent, as 'sent to the fire', so that the count of one thousand and six chests may stand whole.

events.title: No fire in the reading-room before an t-Samhain
events.body: The winter's coal for an Leabharlann comes up the library road smaller and dearer than the year before. The keeper orders no fire in the reading-room before the middle of an t-Samhain and none after dark.

events.title: The mill-race at Muileann chaol runs dry
events.body: The dry year leaves the race at Muileann chaol too low to turn the paper-mill's wheel, and the wheel stands still through the autumn.

events.title: Two surveyors named for the northern inquiry
events.body: At Cathair mhòr Comhairle nam Mèinnean names two of its surveyors, Iain Ruadh mac Nèill, fifty-seven, and Seumas mac Eachainn, twenty-four, to go into the Tuathaich country and learn whether the new fuel burns as men say. The order, countersigned by a clerk of Comhairle na Rìoghachd, bids them report to the Comhairle and send a fair copy to the council's clerk at Cathair dhearg.

events.title: The surveyors cross the boundary stones
events.body: Riding north from Cathair dhearg by the old road, the two surveyors lie a night at the ale-house of Tobar dhomhain and cross the boundary stones on the northern road the next morning. No one at the stones asks their business. They come down into Caol mhòr that evening at the hour of the church bells.

events.title: The maor of Caol mhòr gives the surveyors a letter
events.body: The maor of Caol mhòr, who has asked after the fuel and been told nothing, gives the surveyors a letter to the town. For four days they call on the harbour master, the yards and the market. Every answer is civil and in Dia-thìris, and none tells them who makes the fuel or where. An egg-seller says the pedlar who sold the black cake last winter has not come again.

events.title: The fuel shown burning in the mill yard at Doire ghlas
events.body: Martha Greaves, manager of the great mill of Tional nan Tuathach at Doire ghlas, lets the surveyors see the new fuel burning under the scouring coppers in her yard. Two cakes hold three coppers at the boil through a morning. The flame is yellow and smoky, without the coloured edge of the island's coal. She gives them a cake to take away and will not say who makes it.

events.title: The surveyors burn a cake at Caol mhòr
events.body: In their lodging over a harbour inn at Caol mhòr the surveyors burn half the cake from Doire ghlas in the grate and time it by Iain Ruadh mac Nèill's watch. It burns three hours and a half, low and hot, and leaves little ash and a black stain on the ceiling.

events.title: Iain Ruadh mac Nèill's draft set aside
events.body: Iain Ruadh mac Nèill drafts the report with a closing paragraph that calls the fuel unproven, since the surveyors were shown neither the making nor the maker. Seumas mac Eachainn will not sign it, and writes in its place three plain clauses in Dia-thìris over the old man's account of the road and the yard. Both sign the report, the elder first.

events.title: The fair copy given to the council's clerk
events.body: Seumas mac Eachainn puts the fair copy of the surveyors' report into the hands of the council's clerk at Cathair dhearg and is given a receipt. He waits upon Comhairle na Rìoghachd nearly the whole of an Dàmhair, asking every second morning whether he is wanted. He is not called.

events.title: The surveyors' report filed without minute
events.body: At Cathair mhòr the master of Comhairle nam Mèinnean reads the surveyors' report at his table and passes it to his chief clerk, who files it among the surveys of the year. No minute is made of it and no question asked. Iain Ruadh mac Nèill is sent back to measure the water in the lower galleries of An Sloc Mòr.

events.title: A lamp-lighter's family refused at the council house
events.body: The wife of a lamp-lighter of the south bank of Cathair dhearg, whose husband has lit its lamps nineteen years, brings a petition to the council house asking any work of the town for him now the lamps are to go unlit. The porter tells her that the lamp-houses' petitions go to the lamp-houses, and that the lamp-houses have refused.

events.title: A robbery on the bridge in the first dark night
events.body: On the first night the poorer streets of the capital are left dark, a carter is knocked down on Drochaid Cathair dhearg and his purse taken. The thief runs into the unlit lanes of the south bank. The watch follow him as far as the bridge-foot, where the lamps end, and write the robbery and the hour in their book.

events.title: The surveyors lie at Tobar dhomhain
events.body: On the northern road Seumas mac Eachainn and Iain Ruadh mac Nèill lie a night at Tobar dhomhain, a well, a farm, a smithy and an ale-house, the old surveyor in the one bed and the young one on the bench.

events.title: Harker of Caol mhòr lodges the Board's men
events.body: The Board's surveyors lodge four days at Harker's inn on the harbour at Caol mhòr. They are answered civilly everywhere, in good Dia-thìris, and told nothing of the fuel.

events.title: Iain Ruadh burns a coal of the mountain beside the cake
events.body: In the grate of the inn at Caol mhòr Iain Ruadh mac Nèill lays a thumb of Sloc Mòr coal from his sample-tin on the embers of the northern cake, to show the young surveyor the coloured edge the new fuel lacks.

events.title: Seumas mac Eachainn counts the unlit lamps
events.body: Walking home through the south bank of Cathair dhearg on the night the lamp-houses' order is pinned up, the surveyor counts a hundred and forty-three dark lamps in the lanes, and writes the sum in his gallery-book.

events.title: The Board's report bound in grey board
events.body: The surveyors' report on the northern fuel is bound in the Board's grey board and laid before the council with a single sample-tin of the cake set on its cover.

events.title: The fair court gives up its coal ceiling
events.body: On the day of the last cartload Fionnlagh mac Gille-Chaluim, justice of the fair court at Muileann òg, scrapes the coal ceiling off the painted board at the toll-house door, since no seller keeps it. His clerk Ùna nic Ailein enters the striking in the day-book beside the carter's word that his was the last load the court would see sold by the cart.

events.title: The coal carter of the fair road sells his cart
events.body: Uilleam mac Dhùghaill, who has carried coal down the fair road from the yards of Cathair dhearg for thirty-one years, as his father did before him, sells his cart to a grain carrier of Muileann ghlas. He keeps the horse and comes no more to the fair.

events.title: Coal sold by the sack at the toll-house step
events.body: A man of Cnoc leathan brings eleven sacks of coal on a pack-horse to Muileann òg and sells them one at a time from the step of the toll-house. The fair court allows it, having no rule against it, and enters eleven sales in eleven lines. Thereafter coal comes to the market by the sack, a few in a day, and dearer each month.

events.title: The first coal-lump sold for an altar at the fair
events.body: On Bealltainn a custodian's boy from a small house of Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail in the western hills walks to Muileann òg for a lump of the vein's coal to light the feast-fire, Comhairle nam Mèinnean sending none to houses of its size. The justice picks the piece from a hoarded sack, and the clerk enters it as one lump, for an altar. Four more such sales follow within the year.

events.title: Ùna nic Ailein's letter of the crowning
events.body: Ùna nic Ailein, clerk of the fair court, goes up to Cathair dhearg with half of Muileann òg to see Cathal crowned by Macha's rite, and writes that night to the justice what the street saw: the regalia, the grey mare and the black horse at the temple steps, the king crowned without a word. The letter is kept among the court's papers.

events.title: The coal ink for the new dies
events.body: The mint at Cathair dhearg buys coal of the vein from Comhairle nam Mèinnean to grind the seal-ink for the new reign's dies. Gille-Easbaig Bàn, who cuts them, reckons on the back of the answering letter that the price of the little pot of ink is a year of his wages. The mint pays it, and the recipe on the card by the grinding-stone is kept.

events.title: Cathal's coin comes to the fair
events.body: Through an t-Sultain the first coin of the new dies comes down the fair road in the purses of carriers and drovers. By the opening of Fèill Muileann òg half the coin that crosses the court's table bears Cathal's head, with the coal ink dark at its edge.

events.title: The coal-sellers' row stands empty at the fair
events.body: Fèill Muileann òg runs eleven days and is the thinnest in its clerk's memory. The coal-sellers' row, which once ran the length of the lower field with its wagons, has four booths, two of them selling turf. The booths go dark early for want of fuel to keep a brazier, and Cnoc leathan lets fewer beds.

events.title: Black cake entered at the fair court
events.body: On the northern day of the fair a Tuathach pedlar brings a creel of black cakes made from pit waste. Burned in the court-room stove, it glows hot and stinks. The justice will not have it entered as coal, and the clerk Ùna nic Ailein rules a new page for black cake, of the north, and enters its first sale, to a baker of Muileann ghlas, with the maker not named.

events.title: The foot of the fair court's year
events.body: In the last week of an Dàmhair the clerk of the fair court reckons the year. Under the totals, where the court has always written the weather and the roads, she writes that coal was sold that year by the cart, by the sack and by the lump, and a new fuel once, from the north.

events.title: The coal ceiling scraped from the fair court's board
events.body: Fionnlagh mac Gille-Chaluim, justice of the fair court at Muileann òg, scrapes the painted coal ceiling off the board by the toll-house door, saying there is no sense in keeping a price nobody sells at.

events.title: Uilleam mac Dhùghaill sells his cart
events.body: The last carter of coal on Rathad na Fèille sells his cart to a grain-carrier of Muileann ghlas, keeps his horse, and does not come to the fair again.

events.title: The crowd at the crowning
events.body: Half of Muileann òg goes up the fair road to Cathair dhearg to see Cathal crowned by Macha's rite. Liath Macha and Dubh Sainglenn are led out at the temple steps; the grey mare pulls at her rope.

events.title: A bough hung on a dark lamp-post
events.body: On the evening of the crowning someone hangs a green bough from the feast of Lùnastal on one of the unlit lamp-posts below the tannery in Cathair dhearg.

events.title: The fair court's winter sitting
events.body: The fair court at Muileann òg sits its winter day with three cases of short weight in lamp-fuel and none in coal, the first year the book shows it so.

events.title: Comann nan Sciobairean leases the salt-sheds at Seann Skell
events.body: The company of shipmasters takes a lease of the old salt-sheds on the east side of the harbour at Seann Skell on the southern coast. The sheds have stood empty since the humans' time, the salt trade having gone east, and the town takes the rent gladly. The company brings slack and spoil down the coast in its own hulls and stacks it in the first shed.

events.title: Peigi nic Ascaill sees the works at Seann Skell
events.body: Peigi nic Ascaill, engineer to Comhairle nan Taighean-solais, comes down from Cathair dhearg to see the dubhan works at Seann Skell on the southern coast. She is shown the heaps, the retorts and a lamp burning the new fuel, and the making-shed is kept locked. When she asks where the company learned the making, its master gives her wine.

events.title: Tuathaich hands at the southern works
events.body: The dubhan works at Seann Skell on the southern coast keep Tuathaich hands at the retorts, among them Joe Ashby of Caol mhòr. Five work there in the spring and nine by midsummer. It is rare to see Tuathaich working in the south, and the town's foremen say only that the northern hands know the stuff.

events.title: Peigi nic Ascaill's first report on the new fuel
events.body: Peigi nic Ascaill reports to Comhairle nan Taighean-solais that the new fuel burns clean enough for a lamp and may serve for the five lights, and that the works at Seann Skell will not say how it is made. The report is filed. No answer is written.

events.title: The chimney of Obair-dhubhain Seann Skell finished
events.body: The brick chimney of Obair-dhubhain Seann Skell is finished at the end of the row of salt-sheds. Its smoke lies along the shore on windy days, and the fishwives of the harbour say the herring taste of it. The town petitions the maor against the reek; the maor answers that the company pays its harbour-due, and the petition goes no further.

events.title: A retort bursts at the southern works
events.body: In the summer a retort of the dubhan works at Seann Skell on the southern coast splits along its lower seam, and a hand of the town is scalded on the arm. Peigi nic Ascaill, in the town for the lantern-glass of Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg, draws a baffle for the furnaces and sends it to the works unsigned. The company fits it to every furnace in the row.

events.title: New glass set in the lantern at Tobar dhearg
events.body: The lantern of Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg on the southern cape is fitted with new glass blown at Seann Skell from the white sand of its own shore, at half the price of the capital's glass. Peigi nic Ascaill orders it in an t-Ògmhios and sees it set in an t-Samhain. The tower still burns the island's coal.

events.title: Alasdair mac Ìomhair reads his letter in Brìde's house
events.body: At Seann Skell on the southern coast Alasdair mac Ìomhair, Àrd-choimheadaiche, reads Litir an Àrd-choimheadaiche himself at the evening lamp in the great house of Òrd Bhrìde, on the day it is sent to every house of the order. The hall is full. Many of those who hear it already burn dubhan lamps at home, bought off the works' carts that summer.

events.title: The school at Caol shean disputes Litir an Àrd-choimheadaiche
events.body: The school of Feallsanachd an Fhèidh at Caol shean writes that a fuel made from the vein's own waste cannot be called wholly not coal, since the spoil has lain against the seam for a thousand years. The houses of Òrd an t-Seabhaig round Cnoc bheag write that they did not ask the Àrd-choimheadaiche's opinion and are glad to have it.

events.title: The south-coast boats buy dubhan at Seann Skell
events.body: The fishing boats of the south coast come in to Seann Skell from Tobar dhearg and the coves along the shore to load the works' dubhan for their galley-stoves and riding-lamps. It is cheaper than coal by a third. For five years they have burned driftwood and fish-oil, and more than one boat has gone on the rocks for want of a lamp that would stay lit in a gale.

events.title: The first dubhan barrels go to the lamp-houses of Cathair dhearg
events.body: Eleven carts of six barrels each leave the works at Seann Skell on the southern coast for the lamp-houses of Cathair dhearg, bought on the lamp-houses' account. They are the first dubhan landed at the capital's lamp-houses, for the poorer streets that have been left dark three winters to save coal.

events.title: Peigi nic Ascaill's twenty barrels
events.body: Peigi nic Ascaill buys twenty barrels of dubhan at the works of Comann nan Sciobairean at Seann Skell, entered in the company's ledger to Comhairle nan Taighean-solais on account, without her masters' leave. Joe Ashby chalks a lantern on each barrel. That night she writes asking leave to run a trial of the fuel in a spare lamp below one of the lights for a hundred nights.

events.title: The black ring of the shipmasters
events.body: The hulls of Comann nan Sciobairean bring spoil down the coast to the southern Seann Skell with a black ring painted on their bows, the company's mark.

events.title: The locked making-shed
events.body: At the works at the southern Seann Skell the shed where the dubhan is finished is kept under a padlock the size of a man's fist, opened only for a man with a lamp to go in and out.

events.title: Peigi nic Ascaill's baffle fitted to every furnace
events.body: After a retort bursts at the southern works, a drawing of a baffle for the retort furnaces is sent round unsigned by the engineer of the lights. The company fits it to every furnace in the row, and no retort splits after.

events.title: Joe Ashby chalks the lights' mark
events.body: At the southern works Joe Ashby rolls out twenty barrels held for the engineer of the lights and chalks on each head a square with a flame inside it, the first mark Comhairle nan Taighean-solais ever had.

events.title: The fishwives' petition against the reek
events.body: The town of the southern Seann Skell petitions its maor against the reek of the new works. The maor answers that the company pays its harbour-due, and there the petition ends.
